title: 2 Chronicles 33:10–20
context: Material found only in Chronicles: after Manasseh and his people refuse God’s word, Assyrian commanders take him in chains to Babylon. In distress he humbles himself and prays, God restores him to Jerusalem, and he removes his idols, rebuilds the LORD’s altar, and calls Judah to serve the LORD, though the high places remain. 2 Kings 21 records no repentance; this account is reported as Chronicles gives it. In 33:19 the phrase rendered “the history of Hozai” may also be translated “the history of the seers.”

verses.text: The LORD spoke to Manasseh and to his people, but they didn’t listen.
verses.arminianNotes: “The LORD spoke to Manasseh and to his people, but they didn’t listen.” Arminian readers see God warning before judging, offering real opportunity to turn.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers likewise see God sending his word before judgment falls. The brief statement summarizes what 2 Kings 21:10–15 develops at greater length, and it opens the Chronicler’s distinctive account.

verses.text: Therefore the LORD brought on them the captains of the army of the king of Assyria, who took Manasseh in chains, bound him with fetters, and carried him to Babylon.
verses.arminianNotes: The LORD brings the captains of the king of Assyria, who take Manasseh in chains to Babylon. Arminian readers see judgment designed to humble a proud king and turn him back.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers likewise see God using a foreign power to discipline Manasseh. This episode is found only in Chronicles, and readers in this tradition report it as the book gives it, without supplying historical reconstructions.

verses.text: When he was in distress, he begged the LORD his God, and humbled himself greatly before the God of his fathers.
verses.arminianNotes: “When he was in distress, he begged the LORD his God, and humbled himself greatly before the God of his fathers.” Arminian readers see a genuine turning to God in response to discipline.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers likewise see Manasseh humbled in distress. Many in this tradition see such humbling as the fruit of God’s grace working through affliction, while affirming that Manasseh truly sought God.

verses.text: He prayed to him; and he was entreated by him, and heard his supplication, and brought him again to Jerusalem into his kingdom. Then Manasseh knew that the LORD was God.
verses.arminianNotes: God hears his prayer and restores him, “Then Manasseh knew that the LORD was God.” Arminian readers see God’s mercy toward even the worst of kings when he humbles himself.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers likewise see God’s grace restoring a grievous sinner. Readers in both traditions commonly treat this verse as shared ground: no one is beyond the reach of God’s mercy when they turn to him.

verses.text: Now after this, he built an outer wall to David’s city on the west side of Gihon, in the valley, even to the entrance at the fish gate. He encircled Ophel with it, and raised it up to a very great height; and he put valiant captains in all the fortified cities of Judah.
verses.arminianNotes: Manasseh builds an outer wall to David’s city and places captains in Judah’s fortified cities. Arminian readers see restored responsibility used for the protection of the people.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers likewise see the Chronicler presenting building as a sign of renewed blessing. The topographical details are given as the text has them, and readers in this tradition hold precise identifications with caution.

verses.text: He took away the foreign gods and the idol out of the LORD’s house, and all the altars that he had built in the mountain of the LORD’s house and in Jerusalem, and cast them out of the city.
verses.arminianNotes: He removes the foreign gods and the idol from the LORD’s house and casts out the altars he had built. Arminian readers see repentance expressed in concrete action.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers likewise see the fruit of Manasseh’s humbling. He undoes the very sins described in verses 4–7, showing that his turning involved more than words.

verses.text: He built up the LORD’s altar, and offered sacrifices of peace offerings and of thanksgiving on it, and commanded Judah to serve the LORD, the God of Israel.
verses.arminianNotes: He rebuilds the LORD’s altar, offers peace and thanksgiving offerings, and commands Judah to serve the LORD. Arminian readers see renewed worship and leadership toward faithfulness.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers likewise see a restored king calling the nation back to God. Thanksgiving offerings fit the gratitude of one who had experienced God’s deliverance.

verses.text: Nevertheless the people still sacrificed in the high places, but only to the LORD their God.
verses.arminianNotes: “Nevertheless the people still sacrificed in the high places, but only to the LORD their God.” Arminian readers see reform that was real but incomplete among the people.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers likewise see the limits of Manasseh’s restoration. The Chronicler records honestly that the high places remained, though worship there was directed to the LORD.

verses.text: Now the rest of the acts of Manasseh, and his prayer to his God, and the words of the seers who spoke to him in the name of the LORD, the God of Israel, behold, they are written among the acts of the kings of Israel.
verses.arminianNotes: The rest of Manasseh’s acts, “his prayer to his God, and the words of the seers” are recorded among the acts of the kings of Israel. Arminian readers see the prayer remembered as significant.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers likewise see the Chronicler pointing to fuller records. Readers in this tradition note that the source references here differ from the one given in 2 Kings 21:17.

verses.text: His prayer also, and how God listened to his request, and all his sin and his trespass, and the places in which he built high places and set up the Asherah poles and the engraved images before he humbled himself: behold, they are written in the history of Hozai.
verses.arminianNotes: His prayer, God’s response, his sin, and the places where he built high places “before he humbled himself” are written in the history of Hozai. Arminian readers see both sin and repentance honestly preserved.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers likewise see the record keeping Manasseh’s sin and God’s mercy together. The phrase “before he humbled himself” marks the turning point that shapes the Chronicler’s portrayal.

verses.text: So Manasseh slept with his fathers, and they buried him in his own house; and Amon his son reigned in his place.
verses.arminianNotes: Manasseh dies and is buried in his own house, and Amon reigns. Arminian readers see the end of a reign that included both deep sin and genuine humbling before God.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers likewise see the close of Manasseh’s life. The burial note parallels 2 Kings 21:18, while the Chronicler’s account has given his life a different emphasis.
